transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-12
Start: 09:32 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Aisha Patel (Redwood AE), Marco Ruiz (Redwood SE), Lena Park (NovusAI CTO), Jonas Lee (NovusAI ML Eng), Priya Menon (NovusAI Platform)

Summary:
Redwood AE/SE walk through migration parity for NovusAI which currently uses a mix of OpenAI, Anthropic (Claude variants) and Together models. Focus: API parity (params, streaming, function-calling), embeddings, console features (rollouts, metrics), and Redwood Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization. Customer is evaluating a 1-week pilot for latency and cost comparisons. Security and dedicated/private deployment questions surfaced (SOC2, KMS, SSO).

Topics:
- Model parity mapping (OpenAI/Anthropic/Together -> Redwood)
- API differences: streaming, function-calling, params mapping
- Embeddings migration and vector store considerations
- Console: model catalog, rollouts, metrics, traces
- Redwood Optimize: batching, quantization, cache (K V cash) suggestions
- Private/Dedicated: VPC, KMS/HSM, SOC2, SSO
- Next steps: parity doc, security pack, pilot benchmark

Action items (read out):
- Marco to produce parity mapping and sample requests
- Aisha to share security docs and pricing

Transcript body:
[00:00] Aisha (Redwood AE): Hi everyone, thanks for carving out time, uh I'm Aisha, I'll kick us off. Marco is our solutions engineer, he will run most of the parity demo. Quick around the room?
[00:12] Lena (NovusAI CTO): Hi, Lena here. We're the team that runs the ML inference and product infra, happy to see what Redwood looks like in practice.
[00:18] Jonas (NovusAI ML Eng): Jonas, I own the models and the embedding pipelines.
[00:22] Priya (NovusAI Platform): Priya on platform, mostly interested in VPC/SSO and deployment topology.
[00:27] Marco (Redwood SE): Great, thanks. Goal for today: show how requests you send to OpenAI/Anthropic/Together translate to Redwood API/Console and where we get parity or small mapping changes. We'll also show Optimize recommendations for batching/caching and go over private/dedicated options.
[00:40] Aisha: We're assuming you have a mix of chat + streaming + embeddings, right?
[00:45] Lena: Yeah, chat for product UX, embeddings for search/rerank, and some streaming for preview features. We also do some function calling for structured actions.
[00:53] Marco: Perfect. So first piece: model mapping. For OpenAI gpt-4o/gpt-4 and gpt-3.5 you can map to Redwood-chat-large / Redwood-chat-medium / Redwood-text-legacy respectively. For Anthropic Claude-instant/Claude-2 those map to Redwood-chat-instant and Redwood-chat-2 parity variants; Together's models map similarly — we have pre-verified performance profiles in the catalog. Note: names differ but capability and tokenization are aligned in the catalog.
[01:22] Jonas: Can you show the matrix? We have internal prompts tuned for gpt-4o, need behavior parity.
[01:27] Marco: Yep, I'll pull up the parity sheet. (screen share) Here's the matrix: left column OpenAI model and params, middle Anthropic/Together examples, right column Redwood equivalent and recommended param mapping. Example: OpenAI temperature -> Redwood temperature, max_tokens -> max_tokens, stop -> stop_sequences; function calling maps but the syntax is slightly different — we'll send an example.
[01:48] Jonas: Are the function calling semantics identical? We've got code that depends on 'function_call' field.
[01:54] Marco: Function calling is supported. We expose a 'tools' + 'call' structure; there are a couple small differences like the name of the key for required properties. We'll give a small code snippet you can paste. It's mostly a mechanical translation. 
[02:10] Lena: Streaming — do you do chunked streaming like OpenAI (server-sent events)?
[02:14] Marco: Yes, we support SSE streaming and websocket as well. The streaming frames are the same concept: deltas for choices. There might be minor tokenization differences; we recommend validating with a short sample set.
[02:29] Priya: On embeddings — we use OpenAI embeddings today and store vectors in Pinecone. Any migration gotchas?
[02:34] Marco: Embeddings are straightforward. Redwood returns the same vector floats and dimension equivalents; we provide a small adapter code for Pinecone or your vector DB. Two things to note: batch size -- be mindful of batching defaults; Optimize can suggest batching that improves throughput. Also we have different models for embeddings (semantic vs dense) with profiles showing latency and cost.
[02:56] Jonas: How about similarity? We rely on cosine on 1536-d vectors.
[03:00] Marco: If you're using 1536 dims that's supported — the vector produced will be comparable. We include a verification harness in the pilot to run a recall test across 1k samples.
[03:12] Aisha: Ok I'm going to show the console briefly — model catalog, rollouts and the metrics we surface.
[03:18] Aisha: (navigating) This is the model catalog, you can filter by verified latency profiles, and there's a toggle to pin a model version for a route. Rollouts: canary, A/B, auto-fallback. You get token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route.
[03:36] Lena: Nice, can we see request traces for a single user journey?
[03:39] Aisha: Yes, we'll show traces — here's a trace view with per-turn latencies and the prompt/response. There's also an errors tab with stack traces from the runtime.
[03:51] Jonas: Do you do KV cache? We rely on K V cache to speed up per-turns.
[03:55] Marco: We do K V cache (sometimes transcribed as K V cash in auto transcripts), it's automatic for chat sessions. You can configure TTL and cache keys. It's particularly useful for sessioned chat to reduce repeated attention on earlier tokens.
[04:10] Priya: Security — SOC2, SSO, encryption-at-rest, customer-managed KMS?
[04:15] Aisha: We have SOC2 Type II, ISO on request, SSO with SAML/OIDC, RBAC for console roles. For Private deployments we support bring-your-own KMS/HSM and full VPC peering. We'll send the security pack after the call.
[04:29] Lena: What about data residency? We need EU-only for some customers.
[04:33] Marco: We have region pins and can run private deployments in EU regions or on-prem. For enterprise customers we offer Private with a dedicated control plane.
[04:42] Jonas: Ok, digging into perf — what kind of latency do you target for 2k-token completions?
[04:47] Marco: Depends on hardware and model. On a g4-style or A100 equivalent we typically see 400–800ms per 1k tokens on optimized models in dedicated configs; hosted numbers are a bit higher due to multi-tenant overhead. For strict SLOs we recommend Dedicated reservation. We'll run sample benchmarks in the pilot.
[05:07] Lena: How about cost — we're comparing token cost and infra.
[05:11] Aisha: We show per-token breakdowns; Optimize gives quantization/ batching suggestions that can reduce unit costs 30–60% depending on workload. For example, using int8 quant profiles or batching small requests can drop GPU cycles by half in some patterns.
[05:29] Jonas: Can Redwood do automatic fallbacks if a model is unavailable? We want graceful degradation.
[05:34] Marco: Yes, policies can route to a lower-cost variant or another region; there's auto-fallback to compatible model families. You configure the fallback chain in the route.
[05:44] (30 seconds of screen click, demo of code snippets)
[06:15] Marco: Here's a code snippet translating a OpenAI chat request to Redwood. You see the main pieces: messages -> chat messages, temperature same, max_tokens same, top_p same. For Anthropic style you might map 'instructions' -> system role. For Together there's a small change in how you pass stop sequences.
[06:36] Jonas: Any SDK changes? We use the OpenAI python SDK heavily.
[06:40] Marco: We have official SDKs (python, node) with drop-in helpers. In many places you can swap the client instantiation and keep your call structure the same, but we recommend a thin adapter layer to handle edge cases like function-calling field differences.
[06:57] Priya: How invasive is it to flip from OpenAI to Redwood for our infra? We do millions of small requests/day.
[07:03] Aisha: Many customers run a staged migration: start with non-critical routes, run the pilot to measure latency/cost, then move important routes after validating. For high QPS we recommend testing batching and the autoscale policies on Dedicated.
[07:18] Lena: Let's talk about the pilot — what do you need from us?
[07:22] Marco: Ideally: three sample prompt templates, a traffic sample (keys per minute), and a small evaluation set for quality/regression checks. We'll run a 1-week pilot where we collect latency/cost/recall metrics and run the recall test for embeddings.
[07:37] Jonas: We'll provide that. Also, can SE run the pilot in our EU region?
[07:41] Marco: Yes, we can run in EU regions or in Private if you'd prefer. For EU-only data residency we'd recommend Private/Dedicated.
[07:51] Aisha: Quick note on Optimize: it will analyze your request distribution and suggest batching window sizes, recommended quant profiles, and whether to enable prefix caching. It surfaces estimated cost savings and regression risk.
[08:06] Jonas: How do you measure regression risk? We can't tolerate hallucination regressions.
[08:10] Marco: We tie the quality monitoring to prompt sets and evals. You can pin a baseline and set alerts on quality drift. If a new model/quant profile increases failure rate, Optimize flags it.
[08:25] (short pause, screen changes)
[08:40] Marco: Now demo: here's a sample translation of a streaming OpenAI call to Redwood streaming. Notice we send SSE events, and the client code is almost identical. The biggest mapping is the event names and small differences in the chunk payload.
[09:05] Priya: We have a lot of internal rate-limiting and retries. How do you recommend handling that?
[09:09] Marco: We recommend client-side deps limited with idempotency tokens; Redwood supports request IDs and idempotency headers. On the server side you can also set burst windows and per-route quotas.
[09:22] Lena: Do you log prompts? We need to control PII in logs.
[09:26] Aisha: By default we redact PII in logs, and for Private deployments we can disable persisted transcripts entirely. You can also configure retention window and export options for audit.
[09:39] Jonas: For the parity matrix, will you include exact sample responses? We need to see output diffs.
[09:44] Marco: Yes, the parity doc will include sample prompts and outputs from both sides, plus a small scoring script so you can run automatic diffs.
[09:55] (demo continues showing rollouts, metrics, and a small Optimize report)
[10:30] Marco: I want to highlight a real example: a customer moved chat front-end to Redwood and enabled prefix caching and saw 3x token throughput improvement on the hot path. That's because we cached earlier KV states and reduced re-computation.
[10:47] Lena: Is that caching safe for private data?
[10:50] Marco: You can configure caching to be non-persistent and per-tenant. For Private deployments caching is under your control and can be disabled or encrypted as needed.
[11:03] Jonas: A lot of our inference is reranking heavy — can you run batching for rerank pipelines?
[11:07] Marco: Yes, Optimize can recommend micro-batching for reranks which groups similar requests over a tiny time window. It sometimes increases latency by a few ms but reduces GPU cycles dramatically.
[11:20] (brief crosstalk)
[11:34] Priya: For Dedicated reserved pools — what commitment sizes do you offer?
[11:38] Aisha: We offer monthly and annual reserved capacity, with burst options. We'll follow up with pricing tiers. For pilot we can often provide a small trial pool.
[11:50] Lena: Ok let's call out the risks: model parity and hallucination differences are the main two.
[11:55] Marco: Agreed — that's why we do eval harnesses. We'll run your prompts and compute the quality metrics and surface regressions. If necessary we propose tuning or using a different variant.
[12:08] (silence as Marco runs a quick live test)
[12:45] Marco: Live run done — here's an example output for prompt X from gpt-4o and from Redwood-chat-large; they're similar with minor wording differences. We'll include a batch of 200 samples in the parity doc.
[13:03] Jonas: Great. Any gotchas with tokenization when migrating between Anthropic and OpenAI?
[13:08] Marco: Tokenization differences exist, yes — they can shift token counts. We recommend normalizing to BPE-aware token counters and validating max_tokens. We'll include tokenization notes in the doc.
[13:27] Priya: On the subject of compliance, can you support audit logs being exported to our SIEM?
[13:31] Aisha: Yes, we support syslog export, S3 export, and direct SIEM integrations for audit logs. We'll include the export config in the security pack.
[13:44] Lena: How long to get a pilot running end-to-end?
[13:47] Marco: With the artifacts you said — prompts, sample traffic, and a contact for network (for VPC) — we can start within 3 business days. The pilot itself runs 7–10 days to get stable metrics.
[13:58] Jonas: Nice. For the SDK adapter — do you have open-source examples?
[14:02] Marco: Yes, we have example adapters on github and small migration guides for OpenAI/Anthropic/Together. We'll link those.
[14:12] (silence, background typing)
[14:30] Aisha: Quick recap before we close.
[14:33] Aisha: Action items: Marco will create the parity matrix + sample requests and scoring harness. Aisha will send the security pack and pricing. Jonas will share prompts and traffic sample. We'll schedule pilot kickoff for next week pending materials.
[14:50] Lena: Sounds good. One last Q — do you provide on-call support for pilot incidents?
[14:54] Marco: Yes, SE on-call and a dedicated success manager for pilots.
[14:58] Priya: OK thanks all.
[15:00] Aisha: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up by EOD with links.
[15:05] (call ends)
